<reason>Both sides argued well, but B controlled the decisive clash. B's early reframe on the word "contribute" defused CON's strongest structural argument (that church payment lets the state off the hook) by showing liability is not zero-sum, and CON never fully recovered that line. B's cover-up argument — that transferring known abusers and sealing archives were sovereign institutional choices no truancy law compelled — squarely punctured A's "coerced contractor" frame, and A's answer conceded that a diocese in that position owes money. Given that the motion is itself conditional ("when they played central roles"), that concession largely concedes the principle; A's attempt to recast it as targeted-court-liability versus a blanket levy is a real but secondary distinction about mechanism, and B correctly framed the remainder as accounting rather than principle. B's audit off-ramp also worked as a trap: A accepted transparency but refused to pay whatever enrichment was found, which let B land "you cannot claim poverty and decline to open the books." A's best material — collective punishment of present-day parishioners, the food bank/soup kitchen harm, and the state-as-architect asymmetry — was genuinely forceful and partially blunted by B's asset-versus-pew distinction and the "human shield for the property portfolio" reply. A also gave the sharper closing line ("punishes the choice; the second punishes the cloth"), which kept this competitive. B's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, but the clipped material was peroration rather than argument, and B still made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Question on bishops relocating abusers and sealing archives, and the follow-up in Rebuttal 2, forced A into conceding institutional (diocesan) financial liability — which B then converted in closing into "that is the whole motion," leaving A arguing about mechanism rather than principle.</best_rebuttal>
